subject: English
description: Verb + gerund (-ing) vs verb + to-infinitive; preposition + gerund; common contrasts

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'She enjoys ___ classical music in the evenings.'
questions.explanation: Verbs that take a GERUND (-ing): enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, deny, admit, recommend, postpone, practise, consider, imagine. Distractor 1 — wrong, 'enjoy' does not take an infinitive. Distractor 3 — ungrammatical (you don't say 'to listening'). Distractor 4 — bare verb is wrong after 'enjoys'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'I want ___ a new laptop before the term ends.'
questions.explanation: Verbs that take a TO-INFINITIVE: want, wish, hope, plan, decide, expect, agree, refuse, promise, learn, manage, offer, intend, choose. Distractor 1 — 'want' does not take a gerund. Distractor 3 — bare verb without 'to'. Distractor 4 — ungrammatical.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'He is good at ___ chess in his spare time.'
questions.explanation: After PREPOSITIONS (at, in, on, of, by, for, with, without, after, before), the verb takes the -ING (gerund) form. Examples: 'good at swimming', 'tired of waiting', 'interested in learning', 'before going'. Distractor 1 — infinitive doesn't follow prepositions. Distractor 3 — bare verb is wrong. Distractor 4 — past participle is wrong here.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'My doctor advised me ___ less salt in my meals.'
questions.explanation: When 'advise', 'allow', 'persuade', 'remind', 'warn', 'tell', 'order' have an OBJECT, they take TO-INFINITIVE: 'advised me TO eat'. Without an object, 'advise' takes gerund: 'I advise eating less salt.' Distractor 1 — would be correct only without 'me'. Distractor 3 — bare verb wrong. Distractor 4 — ungrammatical.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: 'He stopped ___ on the way home to admire the sunset.' Choose the correct form for the meaning that he interrupted his journey to look at the sunset.
questions.explanation: 'Stop + gerund' = stop the activity. 'Stop + to-infinitive' = pause IN ORDER TO do something else. Here he paused his journey to look at the sunset → TO-INFINITIVE. Distractor 1 'looking' would mean 'he stopped the activity of looking' — opposite meaning. Distractor 3 — bare verb wrong. Distractor 4 — ungrammatical.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'Would you mind ___ the door for me, please?'
questions.explanation: 'Mind' takes the GERUND. 'Would you mind + V-ing' = polite request. Other gerund-taking verbs: enjoy, suggest, finish, avoid, deny, admit, postpone, practise. Distractor 1 — 'mind' doesn't take infinitive. Distractor 3 — bare verb. Distractor 4 — ungrammatical.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'The new manager made the team ___ overtime last weekend.'
questions.explanation: After 'make', 'let', 'see', 'hear', 'feel' (causative + sense verbs in active voice), use the BARE INFINITIVE (no 'to'). Examples: 'made him laugh', 'let her go', 'saw it fall'. Distractor 1 — common error to add 'to'. Distractor 3 — gerund is wrong with 'made + object'. Distractor 4 — past form wrong here. Note: in PASSIVE voice, 'to' returns: 'He was made TO work overtime.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The volunteers are looking forward to ___ at the national wildlife conservation camp next month.

options.option_text: serve as nature guides for a week
serving as nature guides for a week
have served as nature guides there
served as nature guides for a week

questions.explanation: 'Look forward to' uses 'to' as a preposition, not an infinitive marker, so it must be followed by a gerund (-ing form). 'Serving' is correct. 'Serve' is the most common error — learners mistake the preposition 'to' for the infinitive particle. 'Have served' and 'served' are neither gerunds nor valid completions after a preposition.

questions.stem: The chief fire officer insisted on ___ all exit routes before issuing the safety clearance.

options.option_text: to inspect all exit routes personally

questions.explanation: 'Insist on' is a prepositional verb; 'on' is a preposition requiring a gerund, making 'inspecting' correct. 'To inspect' wrongly treats 'on' as an infinitive marker — the most tempting trap. 'Having inspected' implies the inspection was already completed before the insisting, which contradicts the sentence's forward-looking intent.

questions.stem: After more than a decade in the diplomatic corps, the senior envoy ___ conducting back-channel talks under pressure.

options.option_text: used to conduct such high-stakes talks
is used to conducting back-channel talks
is used to conduct back-channel talks
was using to conduct such sensitive talks

questions.explanation: 'Be used to' means 'be accustomed to' and takes a gerund after 'to' (a preposition here), giving 'is used to conducting'. 'Is used to conduct' is the most tempting wrong answer — learners confuse the prepositional 'to' with the infinitive particle. 'Used to conduct' (without 'be') signals a discontinued past habit, implying the envoy no longer handles such talks, which contradicts the present-tense context.

questions.stem: The nationalised bank regrets ___ that no further deferment of EMI payments will be permissible.

options.option_text: informing all valued customers of this update
to inform all valued customers of this update
inform all valued customers of this update
having informed all customers at an earlier stage

questions.explanation: 'Regret + to-infinitive' is the formal structure for expressing sorrow about something being communicated at this moment. 'Regret + gerund' expresses regret about a past action already taken — e.g., 'I regret sending that email.' Since the bank is making a present policy announcement, 'to inform' is correct. 'Having informed' perversely implies the bank regrets a past act of informing, reversing the intended meaning entirely.

questions.stem: The invigilator forgot ___ the supplementary answer booklets before the examination started.
questions.explanation: 'Forget + to-infinitive' means the person failed to perform the action because they forgot (the action did not happen). 'Forget + gerund' means the action was performed but the memory of it is lost — e.g., 'She forgot locking the door' means she locked it but cannot recall doing so. Since the booklets were never distributed, only 'to distribute' fits the context. 'Distributing' is the most tempting distractor but would imply the booklets were actually handed out.

questions.stem: The seized financial records appeared ___ before the investigating agency could scrutinise them.

options.option_text: to have been tampered with by an unknown party
having been tampered with by an unknown party
to be tampered with by an unknown party
to have tampered with by an unknown party

questions.explanation: 'Appear' requires a to-infinitive complement, ruling out 'having been'. The perfect passive infinitive 'to have been tampered with' is essential because the tampering occurred before the discovery — the sequence demands prior completion. 'To be tampered with' (simple passive) implies current or ongoing action, erasing the crucial time-gap. 'To have tampered with' is active and absurdly implies the records themselves did the tampering.

questions.stem: After outlining the water scarcity crisis, the district collector went on ___ an emergency action plan for the affected talukas.

options.option_text: discussing the water scarcity issue in detail
to present an emergency action plan clearly
to have presented an action plan beforehand
having presented the plan to the officials

questions.explanation: 'Go on + to-infinitive' signals a transition to a new, distinct activity — the collector moved from outlining the problem to presenting solutions. 'Go on + gerund' means continuing the same activity, so 'discussing' (A) implies he kept re-discussing the crisis instead of advancing to remedies — a meaning trap examiners exploit deliberately. 'To have presented' wrongly places the presentation before the outlining. 'Having presented' cannot follow 'go on' in the transitional sense.
